question: Which of the following audit procedures would an auditor be least likely to perform using a generalized computer audit program?

options.A: Searching records of accounts receivable balances for credit balances.
options.B: Investigating inventory balances for possible obsolescence.
options.C: Selecting accounts receivable for positive and negative confirmation.
options.D: Listing of unusually large inventory balances.

question: When an organization uses information technology (IT) extensively, evidence may be available only in electronic form. What is an auditor’s best course of action in such situations?

options.A: Assess the risks of material misstatement as high.
options.B: Use audit software to perform analytical procedures.
options.C: Use generalized audit software to extract evidence from the organization’s databases.
options.D: Perform limited tests of controls over electronic data.

question: An auditor will most likely use computer-assisted audit techniques, rather than manual techniques, when it is necessary to

options.A: Examine all data in an accounts payable file.
options.B: Review approval of dividends.
options.C: Verify unrecorded legal liabilities.
options.D: Assess compliance with policies and procedures related to information security.

question: As part of a fraud audit, a CIA wishes to identify employees with invalid Social Security numbers in the organization’s payroll-transaction data. Which of the following audit tests of controls using computer-assisted audit techniques would best meet the objective?

options.A: Obtaining statistics on the population of the payroll file to identify unusual pay amounts to employees.
options.B: Comparing Social Security numbers paid in the payroll transaction file to a file of government-authorized Social Security numbers.
options.C: Randomly selecting 25 payments from the payroll report and comparing the results to employee Social Security cards in the human resources records.
options.D: Comparing the payroll transaction file to the employee master file to extract payments to employees who are not in the employee master file.

question: Which of the following statements concerning the parallel simulation approach when testing a computerized accounting system is true?

options.A: Transactions are reprocessed only by the organization’s computer programs.
options.B: Transactions from throughout the period may be reprocessed.
options.C: Only fictitious transactions are reprocessed.
options.D: It tends to be a cost-effective method.

question: Which of the following statements is true about the integrated test facility (ITF) method for testing a computerized accounting system?

options.A: ITF reprocesses only actual, not fictitious, transactions.
options.B: The test transactions must be submitted with the computer operator’s knowledge.
options.C: ITF tests the actual program in operation.
options.D: ITF is used extensively by internal auditors.

question: An auditor obtains a digital file that contains the dollar amounts of all the organization’s inventory items by style number. The auditor is aware that certain inventory styles are held on consignment for others. The auditor can best ascertain that the inventory is not overstated by using a computer program that

options.A: Statistically selects samples of all amounts.
options.B: Tests for and accumulates all amounts for items with style numbers indicating consigned merchandise.
options.C: Mathematically calculates the extension of each style quantity by the unit price.
options.D: Prints on paper the information that is on the file.

question: An auditor who wishes to capture an entity’s data as transactions are processed and continuously test the entity’s computerized information system most likely would use which of the following techniques?

options.A: Snapshot application.
options.B: Embedded audit module.
options.C: Integrated data check.
options.D: Test data generator.

question: Which of the following computer-assisted auditing techniques processes an organization’s input data on a controlled program under the auditor’s control to test controls in the computer system?

options.A: Test data.
options.B: Review of program logic.
options.C: Integrated test facility.
options.D: Parallel simulation.

question: When an auditor tests the internal controls of a computerized system, which of the following is true of the test data approach?

options.A: Test data are coded to a dummy subsidiary so they can be extracted from the system under actual operations conditions.
options.B: Test data programs need not be tailor-made by the auditor for each computer application.
options.C: Test data programs usually consist of all possible valid and invalid conditions regarding compliance with internal controls.
options.D: Test data are processed with the organization’s program and the results are compared to the auditor’s predetermined results.

question: Which of the following is a computer-assisted audit technique that permits an auditor to insert the auditor’s version of an organization’s program to process data and compare the output with the organization’s output?

options.A: Test data module.
options.B: Frame relay protocol.
options.C: Remote node router.
options.D: Parallel simulation.

question: Management of Company X has made representations regarding certain edit checks in the payroll processing program. One such representation is that a reasonableness test is performed on the accounting for overtime hours. The auditor decides to test the effectiveness of this control by creating test transactions, some of which contain material errors. The auditor then compares the test and actual results. This procedure is

options.A: Parallel simulation.
options.B: The test data approach.
options.C: Possible only with an embedded audit module.
options.D: The integrated test facility method.

question: Which computer auditing method uses a set of dummy transactions to test controls in processing programs?

options.A: Test data approach.
options.B: Parallel simulation.
options.C: Integrated test facility.
options.D: Embedded audit module.

question: What is the primary advantage of parallel simulation?

options.A: It provides for continuous monitoring of online, real-time systems.
options.B: Processing is tested at one moment in time.
options.C: Any transactions during the period may be reprocessed.
options.D: It tests the controls directly.

question: An internal auditor at a retail chain wants to determine how effectively store locations are enforcing return policies. Which computer-assisted audit technique (CAAT) should the auditor primarily use to assess compliance?

options.A: Duplicate identification to ensure all returns are single instances.
options.B: Gap identification to find missing entries in the return logs.
options.C: Stratification to organize customer feedback by dissatisfaction levels.
options.D: Data mining to extract patterns related to deviations in return transactions.

question: An internal auditor at a healthcare organization identifies anomalies in employee overtime payments through the use of computer-assisted audit techniques (CAATs). Which action should follow this discovery to ensure the audit addresses potential issues adequately?

options.A: Report the finding to all employees to ensure transparency.
options.B: Analyze the anomalies further to determine whether they result from errors or potential fraud.
options.C: Terminate the audit process and redo the initial assessment with different tools.
options.D: Conduct interviews with external auditors to validate the findings.

question: During an audit, an internal auditor selects data analytics as the primary tool for examining payroll expenses. Which of the following steps should the auditor take first in the data analytics process?

options.A: Inform management about the data analytics tools that will be used.
options.B: Obtain relevant data for analysis.
options.C: Analyze the data to identify patterns or anomalies.
options.D: Define objectives and key performance indicators (KPIs).

question: While using a flowchart to assess a business process, an auditor notices tasks that could be automated with technological tools. Which recommendation is most consistent with enhancing efficiency through technology?

options.A: Implement organization-wide IT training sessions.
options.B: Outsource the process to a third-party provider.
options.C: Introduce robotic process automation (RPA).
options.D: Develop a new standard operating procedure (SOP) for the tasks.

question: An internal auditor is tasked with identifying potential areas of fraud in an organization’s accounts payable system. Which computer-assisted audit technique (CAAT) would be most effective?

options.A: Analysis of payment methods used over the last year.
options.B: Duplicate payment detection analysis.
options.C: Manual review of vendor agreements.
options.D: Comparison of purchasing patterns to employee schedules.

question: When preparing for an audit engagement of a large multinational bank, the internal auditor decides to use computer-assisted audit techniques (CAATs) to improve the information gathering process. Which of the following is a common feature of CAATs?

options.A: Increased auditing time by performing rigorous manual checks.
options.B: Limited analysis to small, easily manageable sample sets.
options.C: Access to an organization’s complete database for thorough analysis.
options.D: Reliance on physical documentation for data verification.

question: An internal auditor in a governmental agency is exploring the use of AI to enhance audit procedures. What is one key benefit of incorporating AI in auditing practices?

options.A: AI performs automated reviews, identifying risk areas faster than traditional methods.
options.B: AI completely replaces the need for auditors.
options.C: AI guarantees 100% accurate financial forecasts.
options.D: AI allows auditors to bypass understanding complex datasets.

question: In an internal audit engagement involving data analytics, an auditor is using automated tools to analyze employee expense reports for anomalies. What is an advantage of using these tools in this context?

options.A: They can replace the entire internal audit team, thus saving costs.
options.B: They allow the auditor to review all data rather than sampling, increasing the chances of identifying anomalies.
options.C: They guarantee the identification of fraudulent activities.
options.D: They remove the need for any further analysis or judgment by the auditor.

question: During the audit of a financial institution, an internal auditor is assessing the use of data mining to detect fraudulent activities. Which of the following is a key benefit of using data mining techniques in fraud detection?

options.A: It eliminates the need for manual reviews.
options.B: It allows for the exploration of large datasets to find unusual patterns indicating fraud.
options.C: It ensures that no fraudulent activities occur in the future.
options.D: It provides instant results with 100% accuracy.

question: An expert system

options.A: Comprises a general ledger/financial reporting system and a management reporting system.
options.B: Is a central database for transaction-level data.
options.C: Solicits opinions from experts, summarizes the opinions, and feeds the summaries back to the experts.
options.D: Is useful in solving unstructured problems.

question: A bank implemented an expert system to help account representatives consolidate the bank’s relationships with each customer. The expert system has

options.A: A sequential control structure.
options.B: Distinct input-output variables.
options.C: A knowledge base.
options.D: Passive data elements.

question: Which of the following features is classified as part of an expert system?

options.A: Use of email to route and approve purchase requisitions.
options.B: Automatic obligation of budget funds as soon as an order is issued.
options.C: Issuance of purchase requisition notices as soon as the on-hand balance reaches the reorder point.
options.D: Automatic placement of orders with suppliers who currently offer the best combination of price, freight cost, and delivery time.

question: The purchasing department buys cleaning compound from four different companies. The computerized purchasing system uses a decision table to select a vendor based on continually changing costs, delivery dates, and past experience. This is an example of a(n)

options.A: Base case system evaluation.
options.B: Expert system.
options.C: Parallel simulation.
options.D: Chargeback system.

question: Which one of the following incorporates making the best decisions possible, using a logical approach by asking a series of questions, by using reasoning, and by allowing subjective inputs and outputs?

options.A: Decision support systems.
options.B: Expert systems.
options.C: Multi-networking.
options.D: Teleprocessing.

question: A group of processing units working together to process information much like the human brain, including learning from previous situations and generalizing concepts, is a(n)

options.A: Neural network.
options.B: Case-based reasoning system.
options.C: Rule-based expert system.
options.D: Intelligent agent.

question: Which one of the following statements concerning concurrent auditing techniques is false?

options.A: They allow monitoring a system on a continuous basis for fraudulent transactions.

options.C: They allow faster detection of unauthorized transactions.
options.D: They are standard components of generic software packages.

question: What is a primary characteristic of tasks suitable for robotic process automation (RPA)?

options.A: Complex instructions requiring human interpretation.

options.C: Rules-based and repetitive tasks.
options.D: Tasks with subjective decision making.

question: For which of the following computer-assisted auditing techniques does the auditor use a controlled program?

options.A: Integrated test facility.
options.B: Parallel simulation.
options.C: Test data approach.
options.D: Program code checking.

question: An organization wants to improve audit efficiency by automating repetitive tasks, such as invoice matching and compliance checks. What technology should be implemented?

options.A: Automated process tools to streamline rule-based tasks.
options.B: Spreadsheet-based macros to assist with compliance calculations.
options.C: Workflow automation software to route approvals efficiently.
options.D: Data analytics tools to identify anomalies in financial transactions.

question: Continuous monitoring auditing techniques are beneficial to the audit process because they provide for which of the following?

options.A: Ease of access to systems and records.
options.B: Ability of auditors to analyze large amounts of data.
options.C: Ease of training for auditors.
options.D: Ability of auditors to deploy software solutions quickly.

question: In an analysis of operational data across diverse departments, an internal auditor identifies inconsistent reporting standards. Which tool can aid in standardizing data collection and facilitate comparative analysis?

options.A: A spreadsheet template.
options.B: A block diagram.

options.D: An action diagram.

question: Which of the following is most likely to help coordinate review of engagement workpapers?

options.A: Digitization.
options.B: Subject-matter titles.
options.C: Results of analyses.
options.D: Summaries.

question: Which of the following conditions constitutes inappropriate preparation of workpapers?

options.A: All forms and directives used by operational management are included in the workpapers.

options.D: Tick marks are explained in notes.

question: Engagement workpapers are indexed by means of reference numbers. The primary purpose of indexing is to

options.B: Support the final engagement communication.
options.C: Eliminate the need for follow-up reviews.
options.D: Determine that workpapers adequately support findings, conclusions, and recommendations.

question: Which of the following is the most important if workpapers are to have the characteristics that will ensure that they achieve their primary purposes?

options.A: Workpapers must be of standard format and standard content.
options.B: Workpapers must be properly indexed and cross-referenced to the draft final engagement communication.
options.C: Workpapers must provide sufficient, reliable, and useful information to support the engagement results.
options.D: Workpapers must be arranged in logical order following the engagement work program sequence.

options.A: Efficiently.
options.B: Professionally.

question:
An internal auditor prepared a workpaper that consisted of a list of employee names and identification numbers as well as the following statement:

By matching random numbers with employee identification numbers, 40 employee personnel files were selected to verify that they contain all documents required by the organization’s policy 501. No exceptions were noted.

options.A: Use of tick marks to show that each file was examined.
options.B: Removal of the employee names to protect their confidentiality.
options.C: Justification for the sample size.
options.D: Listing of the actual documents examined for each employee.

question: The internal audit function’s engagement workpapers must be reviewed. To facilitate the review, the most fundamental method is

options.A: Cross-referencing.
options.B: Indexing.
options.C: Verification symbols.

question: The internal auditor prepares workpapers primarily for the benefit of

options.A: The external auditor.

question: An internal auditor’s workpapers should support the findings, conclusions, and recommendations to be communicated. One of the purposes of this requirement is to

question: During the workpaper review, an internal auditing supervisor finds that the internal auditor’s findings are not adequately cross-referenced to supporting documentation. The supervisor will most likely instruct the internal auditor to

options.C: Eliminate any cross-references to other workpapers because the system is unclear.
options.D: Provide a cross-referencing system that shows the relationship among findings, conclusions, recommendations, and the related facts.

question: An internal auditor’s workpapers should be reviewed by the

options.A: Management of the activity under review.
options.B: Management of the internal audit function.
options.C: Audit committee of the board.
options.D: Management of the organization’s security division.

question: Which of the following does not describe one of the functions of engagement workpapers?

options.A: Facilitates third-party reviews.
options.B: Aids in the planning, performance, and review of engagements.
options.C: Provides the principal support for engagement communications.
options.D: Aids in the professional development of the operating staff.

question: A workpaper is complete when it

options.A: Complies with the internal audit function’s format requirements.
options.B: Contains all of the attributes of an observation.
options.C: Is clear, concise, and accurate.
options.D: Satisfies the engagement objective for which it is developed.

question: The primary purpose of an internal auditor’s workpapers is to

options.A: Provide documentation of the planning and execution of engagement procedures performed.
options.B: Serve as a means with which to prepare the financial statements.
options.C: Document weaknesses in internal control with recommendations to management for improvement.
options.D: Comply with the Standards.

question: The primary purpose of an engagement workpaper prepared in connection with payroll expense is to

question: Which of the following most completely describes the appropriate content of workpapers?

options.A: Engagement objectives, procedures, and conclusions.
options.B: Engagement purposes, criteria, techniques, and recommendations.
options.C: Engagement objectives, procedures, observations, conclusions, and recommendations.
options.D: Engagement subject, purposes, sampling information, and analysis.

question: Engagement workpapers include

options.A: Providing a basis for evaluating the internal audit quality program.
options.B: Copies of all source documents examined in the course of the engagement.
options.C: Copies of all procedures that were reviewed during the engagement.
options.D: All workpapers prepared during a previous engagement performed in the same area.

question: The chief audit executive establishes policies for

options.A: Standardized workpapers.
options.B: Defining the hours available for individual engagements.
options.C: Defining standardized tick marks and ensuring compliance with them.
options.D: Ensuring the written documentation of all conversations held throughout the engagement.

question: An adequately documented workpaper should

options.A: Be concise but complete.
options.B: Follow a unique form and arrangement.
options.C: Contain examples of all forms and procedures used by operational management.
options.D: Not contain copies of operational management records.

question:
Productivity statistics are provided quarterly to the board of directors. An internal auditor checked the ratios and other statistics in the four most recent reports. The internal auditor wrote a note for the workpapers describing these procedures and then discarded the scratch paper and report copies. The note stated,

The ratios and other statistics in the quarterly reports to the board were checked for the last 4 quarters and appropriate supporting documents were examined. All amounts appear to be appropriate.

In this situation,

options.A: Four quarters do not provide a large enough sample on which to base a conclusion.
options.B: The internal auditor’s workpapers are not sufficient to facilitate an efficient review of the internal auditor’s work.
options.C: The internal auditor should have included the scratch paper in the workpapers.
options.D: The internal auditor did not consider whether the information in the report to the board was compiled efficiently.

question: Employees using personal computers have been reporting occupational injuries and claiming substantial workers’ compensation benefits. The workpapers of an engagement performed to determine the extent of the organization’s exposure to such personal injury liability should include

options.A: Analysis of claims by type of equipment and extent of use by individual employees.
options.B: Confirmations from insurance carriers as to claims paid under workers’ compensation policies in force.
options.C: Reviews of documentation supporting purchases of personal computers.
options.D: Listings of all personal computers in use and the employees who use them.

question: Which of the following is an unnecessary feature of a workpaper prepared in connection with maintenance costs?

options.A: The internal auditor has initialed and dated the workpaper as of the date completed even though the workpaper was prepared over the preceding 4 working days.
options.B: Total repair expense for the month preceding the engagement is shown.
options.C: The chief audit executive has initialed the workpaper as reviewer although the workpaper was prepared by another person.
options.D: Total acquisition cost of property, plant, and equipment for the preceding month is shown.

question: When performing an engagement to evaluate the computerized purchasing activities of a manufacturing organization, which of the following should be included in the permanent file portion of the engagement workpapers?

options.A: Copies of the computer program documentation.

options.C: Prior year’s workpapers revised to reflect changes during the current year.
options.D: Information concerning administrative controls over the computer operations at each location.

question: Each individual workpaper should, at a minimum, contain a(n)

options.D: Descriptive heading.

question: Internal auditors often include summaries within their workpapers. Which of the following best describes the purpose of such summaries?

options.A: Summaries are prepared to conform with the Standards.

options.C: Summaries distill the most useful information from several workpapers into a more usable form.

question: When engagement conclusions are challenged, the internal auditor’s factual rebuttal is best facilitated by

options.D: Explicit procedures in the engagement work program.

question: Which type of workpaper summary is typically used to consolidate numerical data scattered among several schedules?

options.A: Statistical summaries.
options.B: Segment summaries.
options.C: Results summaries.
options.D: Pyramid summaries.

question: This workpaper will be considered deficient if which other relevant engagement workpaper is not cross-referenced and included in the cash section of the workpaper file?

options.A: Petty cash count.

question: A deficiency in this workpaper is that

question: Which of the following concepts distinguishes the retention of computerized audit documentation from the traditional hard copy form?

options.B: Evidential support for all findings is copied and provided to local management during the closing conference and to each person receiving the final report.
options.C: Computerized data files can be used in computer audit procedures.
options.D: Audit programs can be standardized to eliminate the need for a preliminary survey at each location.

question: Workpaper summaries, if prepared, can be used to

options.A: Promote efficient workpaper review by internal audit supervisors.
options.B: Replace the detailed workpaper files for permanent retention.
options.C: Serve as an engagement final communication to senior management.
options.D: Document the full development of engagement observations and recommendations.

question: An internal auditor’s findings may be contested by management. The most effective response is likely that supported by

options.A: Indexation of engagement observations.
options.B: Sources of information.
options.C: The engagement work program.
options.D: Pro forma workpapers.

question: During an organization’s audit planning phase, the chief audit executive decides to implement a new standardized workpaper system. How should the audit team approach this change to ensure a successful transition?

options.A: Immediately adapt to the new system without considering previous workpapers.
options.B: Perform a phased introduction to allow time for auditors to familiarize themselves with the system.
options.C: Implement the new system for select engagements initially to test its effectiveness.
options.D: Provide training sessions and consider team feedback for adjustments during implementation.

question: While compiling audit workpapers in an IT audit, an internal auditor discovers that some workpapers are missing cross-references for certain findings. What is the best course of action to correct this oversight?

options.A: Assume significance is minimal and continue with existing documentation.

question: An audit intern is preparing workpapers for a small organization’s audit engagement. question: During an internal audit engagement at a large technology firm, the internal auditors discovered several discrepancies in the implementation of IT controls. question: In a healthcare compliance audit, the internal audit team is evaluating the effectiveness of patient privacy controls. options.A: Ensure the findings are documented and cross-referenced and that detailed analyses are included in the workpapers.
options.B: Collaborate with the organization’s legal team to address the awareness of privacy breaches.
options.C: Notify the whistleblower of the audit findings and actions taken.
options.D: Immediately discuss the matter with external auditors for a third-party evaluation of the breach.

question: In evaluating whether workpapers adequately support an engagement, what criterion should an auditor consider to ensure they are sufficient?

options.A: Conciseness and brevity of the documented information.
options.B: Accessibility and ease of use for external parties.
options.C: The number of documented findings.
options.D: The relevance and reliability of the information contained.

question: A new auditor on the internal audit team questions the purpose of including detailed descriptions in workpapers. How would you explain the importance of detailed descriptions to this auditor?

options.C: The details allow workpapers to remain unchanged for external review.

question: In preparing workpapers for review, an internal auditor uses electronic tools to ensure efficiency. What is a principal advantage of using electronic workpapers compared to traditional manual methods? Electronic workpapers

options.A: Enhance security by automatically preventing unauthorized access.
options.B: Allow for more flexible workpaper formats during engagements.
options.C: Provide easier cross-referencing and search functionality.
options.D: Automatically change retention policies, making them more detailed by default.

question: During an audit engagement at a manufacturing organization, the internal auditor notices that certain workpapers lack cross-references to other relevant documents. Why is it problematic for workpapers to lack cross-references?

options.A: It makes the workpapers less organized and may impair the review process.
options.B: It renders the workpapers inaccessible by external auditors.
options.C: It increases the risk of unauthorized access to workpapers.
options.D: It indicates a lack of objectivity in the audit findings.

question: An internal audit team is reviewing the workpapers of a previous engagement within the finance department of a retail chain. They find several instances of missing cross-references. What should the team do to rectify this issue?

options.A: Ignore the missing cross-references and focus on the content quality.
options.B: Remove the sections with missing cross-references because they are unreliable.
options.C: Verify whether the cross-references added are necessary and justified.
options.D: Add the cross-references using the expected format to ensure all findings are linked to supporting data.

question: An internal audit team is reviewing the documentation prepared for an engagement at an insurance organization. options.C: Immediately finalize and file the workpapers to avoid project delays.
options.D: Use the confusing workpapers as a learning point in its next training session without making changes.

question: An internal auditor performing a financial audit is analyzing discrepancies in cash flow statements and needs to summarize the relevant facts about the findings. Which method of workpaper organization can help the auditor provide a concise overview of the most important information for review?

options.A: Compiling all raw data into one document.
options.B: Creating a segment summary for each section of the workpapers.
options.C: Arranging documents in chronological order of events.
options.D: Indexing each document for easy reference.

question: An internal auditor is finalizing the engagement report and must ensure all conclusions are well supported. The audit identified a significant control deficiency. Which element of the workpapers is most critical to justifying the conclusion?

options.A: The index or reference number of the workpapers.
options.B: The summary of interviews and surveys.
options.C: The engagement planning documentation.
options.D: The cross-referencing of findings to the related workpapers.

question: A consulting firm has recently adopted electronic audit workpapers to improve its auditing efficiency. What is a potential advantage of using electronic workpapers over traditional paper-based methods?

options.A: Reduced need for data backup and security features.
options.B: Improved collaboration through digital file sharing.
options.C: Audit findings access limited to the internal audit function.
options.D: Decreased reliance on IT infrastructure.

question: An audit workpaper includes a list of transactions and the results of the testing undertaken. What is missing to make the workpaper complete?

options.A: A reference to a prior audit where similar sampling was performed.
options.B: The total number of transactions from which the sample was taken.
options.C: A description of the sampling methodology applied during the audit.
options.D: A general statement that the transactions appeared appropriate.

question: An auditor is preparing a workpaper to document a control weakness. What should be included to ensure the workpaper is sufficient?

options.A: A description of the issue, supporting evidence, and the impact on the organization.
options.B: A brief statement that the control weakness was noted.
options.C: A summary of similar weaknesses found in previous audits.
options.D: A reference to general industry best practices.

question: An audit team is compiling workpapers for a completed engagement. What should be checked to confirm they contain sufficient evidence?

options.A: That there is a clear conclusion for each test.
options.B: Inclusion of evidence for high-risk findings, evidence should be proportionate with risk.
options.C: There is a working paper written and retained for each test.
options.D: The presence of clear audit procedures, findings, and supporting documentation.

question: An auditor is reviewing workpapers for completeness before finalizing the engagement report. What must be present to ensure they are sufficient?

options.A: A collection of informal auditor notes summarizing key observations.
options.B: A description of audit steps performed, along with procedural details.
options.C: A record of key documents, supporting evidence, and justification for conclusions.
options.D: A high-level summary of findings with limited supporting data.

question: An internal audit team identifies control deficiencies in procurement practices. How should the workpapers be linked to the engagement results?

options.A: Referencing employee feedback on the procurement processes.
options.B: Describing the nature of deficiencies and how they impact procurement controls.
options.C: Providing a summary of procurement processes along with identified weaknesses.
options.D: Documenting testing procedures, evidence, and conclusions related to the deficiencies.

question: Which of the following is a good practice for workpapers used in support of the internal auditor’s report?

options.A: Workpapers should be kept secure from everyone except other internal auditors to ensure transparency.
options.B: Workpapers should be organized chronologically, i.e., with the papers prepared earliest at the front of the file.
options.C: Workpapers should be sufficient to support the internal auditor’s report without additional verbal elaboration by the auditor.
options.D: Internal auditors in a given organization should be encouraged to develop their own methods for organization and documentation.

question: Workpapers for a bank reconciliation engagement should include (either directly or through cross-reference) which of the following?

options.A: List of all deposits made during the period in question.
options.B: Set of self-explanatory tick marks.
options.C: List of outstanding and cashed checks.
options.D: Cash balance per the general ledger as of the reconciliation date.

question: A new internal auditor assigned to an engagement in process was able to fully comprehend the engagement from the workpapers and bring the engagement to a successful conclusion. This best demonstrates that the workpapers were which of the following?

options.A: Understandable.
options.B: Complete.
options.C: Logically arranged.
options.D: Sufficient.

question: Internal auditors use a variety of indexing and cross-referencing methods in their audit workpapers. A chief audit executive (CAE) might devise an indexing method for workpapers tailored to a specific organization’s needs. On the other hand, a government audit agency might devise one method for all organizations under the agency’s jurisdiction. Which of the following best explains the reason for this difference between the two indexing methods?

options.A: The CAE devises a method that simplifies the review process in a particular organization, but the government audit agency devises one uniform method to simplify the review process of the vastly different organizations to be audited.
options.B: The method of the CAE is prescribed by the Global Internal Audit Standards, but the method of the government audit agency is required by agency policy.
options.C: The method of the CAE is prescribed by the Global Internal Audit Standards, but the method of the government audit agency is required by law.
options.D: The CAE devises a method that is specified by the organization’s audit committee, but the government audit agency devises one uniform method that is required by law.

question: The internal auditor is most likely to make workpapers available to management of the activity under review when

options.A: Fraud is suspected.
options.B: The internal auditors have recorded specific damaging comments.
options.C: The internal auditor considers the content noncontroversial.
options.D: Operational management comments are needed to evaluate significance and accuracy.

question: When current-file workpapers are no longer of use to the internal audit function, they should be

options.A: Destroyed.
options.B: Placed in the custody of the organizational legal department for safekeeping.
options.C: Transferred to the permanent file.
options.D: Transferred to the custody of operational management for ease of future records.

question: An internal audit supervisor is reviewing the engagement workpapers prepared by the staff. Which of the following review comments is true?

options.A: Each workpaper should include the actual and the budgeted times related to such engagement work.
options.B: Including copies of all the forms and directives of operational management constitutes over-documentation.
options.C: Conclusions need not be documented in the workpapers when the engagement objectives are achieved.
options.D: Each workpaper should include a statement regarding operational management’s cooperation.

question: When reviewing engagement workpapers, the primary responsibility of an engagement supervisor is to determine that

options.A: Each worksheet is properly identified with a descriptive heading.
options.B: Workpapers are properly referenced and kept in logical groupings.
options.C: Standard internal audit function procedures are adhered to with regard to workpaper preparation and technique.
options.D: Workpapers adequately support the engagement findings, conclusions, and recommendations.

question: The internal audit function’s workpapers

options.A: Are protected from disclosure in civil but not criminal legal matters.
options.B: Are protected from disclosure in criminal but not civil legal matters.
options.C: Are protected from disclosure in civil and criminal legal matters.
options.D: Generally are not protected from disclosure in legal matters.

question: The chief audit executive’s (CAE’s) responsibility for engagement records is to

options.A: Release them to external parties upon request.
options.B: Control access.
options.C: Seek their review by the external auditors.
options.D: Obtain management’s opinion on compliance with the law.

question: The internal audit function’s policy regarding notes made by a reviewer of workpapers most likely is to

options.A: Discard the notes after questions are identified.
options.B: Retain the notes until they have served their purpose.
options.C: Include the notes in the permanent file.
options.D: Follow the retention requirements of the relevant legal environment for workpapers.

question: Workpapers contain a record of engagement work performed and much confidential information. They are the property of the organization and remain under control of the internal audit function, which is responsible for their security. Which of the following is the most important control requirement for workpapers?

options.A: Allow access to workpapers only to internal audit function personnel.
options.B: Provide for the protection of workpapers at all times and to the extent appropriate.
options.C: Make the administrative section of the internal audit function responsible for the security of workpapers.
options.D: Purge workpapers periodically of materials that are considered confidential.

question: Which of the following actions constitutes a violation of the confidentiality concept regarding workpapers? An internal auditor

options.A: Takes workpapers to his or her hotel room overnight.
options.B: Shows workpapers on occasion to operational management.
options.C: Allows the external auditor to copy workpapers.
options.D: Misplaces workpapers occasionally.

question: The primary objective of maintaining security over workpapers is to

options.A: Prohibit unauthorized changes or removal of information.
options.B: Prohibit operational management from seeing workpapers.
options.C: Facilitate subsequent engagements in the same department.
options.D: Facilitate engagements by external auditors.

question: A fire destroyed a large portion of an organization’s inventory. Management is filing an insurance claim and needs to use the internal auditors’ workpapers in preparing the claim. Management

options.A: May not use the workpapers in preparing the claim.
options.B: May use the workpapers in preparing the claim, but such use should be approved by the chief audit executive.
options.C: Should be precluded from preparing the claim, and this function should be performed by the internal audit function.
options.D: May use the workpapers in preparing the claim, but such use should be approved by the organization’s external auditors.

question: Workpapers should be disposed of when they are of no further use. Retention policies must

options.A: Specify a minimum retention period of 3 years.
options.B: Be prepared by the audit committee.
options.C: Be approved by legal counsel.
options.D: Be approved by the external auditor.

question: Which of the following states an inappropriate policy relating to the retention of engagement workpapers?

options.A: Workpapers should be disposed of when they have no further use.
options.B: Workpapers prepared for fraud investigators should be retained indefinitely.
options.C: Workpaper retention schedules should be approved by legal counsel.
options.D: Workpaper retention schedules should consider legal and contractual requirements.

question: The best description of the principal purpose for retaining workpapers is to

options.A: Help perform the engagement in an orderly fashion.
options.B: Maintain the engagement work program for reuse in the next engagement.
options.C: Provide support for the final engagement communication.
options.D: Provide a basis for supervisory review.

question: An internal audit function’s policies regarding engagement records should address such matters as their content, retention period, handling of access requests, and responsibility for control and security. options.C: Records created with an expectation of confidentiality are protected from disclosure.

question: Engagement workpapers are reviewed to ensure that

question: Which of the following is true regarding proper control of workpapers?

options.A: Auditors have the equivalent of attorney-client privilege.
options.B: Engagement records are the property of the auditor.
options.C: Prevent unauthorized changes or removal of information.
options.D: All internal audit personnel have access to engagement records.

question: Which of the following statements about an internal auditor’s workpapers is true?

options.A: Workpapers are the only means that can be used to support an engagement conclusion.

question: Security over the internal audit function’s workpapers is primarily directed toward

options.A: Unauthorized changes in the information obtained.

options.C: Prevention of access by operational management.
options.D: Prevention of access by external parties.

question: The internal audit function’s retention requirements for engagement records must be developed by the

question: The internal audit function’s retention requirements for engagement records

options.B: Provide for destruction of some but not all workpapers.
options.C: Vary with the media in which they are stored.
options.D: Tend to be similar among legal environments.

question: An organization’s internal audit department wants to establish better policies regarding the retention of electronic workpapers. What guideline should it consider following to ensure compliance and security?

options.A: Retain all electronic workpapers indefinitely for all audit engagements.
options.B: Create a retention policy based on the average retention timelines of peer organizations.
options.C: Establish a retention policy in collaboration with legal counsel, considering organizational needs and regulatory requirements.

question: An internal audit team is reviewing workpapers related to a financial institution’s compliance procedures. They find that the documentation lacks a clear statement of the procedures tested. How should the audit team address this issue?

options.A: Note the deficiency and inform the team lead for potential follow-up.
options.B: Complete the documentation without re-performance verification.
options.C: Discard these workpapers because they cannot be verified.
options.D: Share the concern with operational management to rectify the documentation.

question: During the audit of a healthcare organization, the need arises to indefinitely retain workpapers related to a recent audit. What practical step should be taken to ensure the workpapers are properly retained and accessible?

options.A: Store them in the organization’s physical archive.
options.B: Use electronic storage with proper backups.
options.C: Retain only the physical copies due to their authenticity.
options.D: Share copies with the organization’s entire management team.

question: You are designing a policy on the retention of workpapers for your organization. Which factor is essential to ensure compliance and effective documentation management?

options.A: Ensure all past workpapers are retained indefinitely.

options.C: Develop a policy approved by an external auditor.

question: An internal auditor must determine which personnel have access to certain confidential workpapers. What is the primary reason for controlling access to these workpapers?

options.A: To abide by organizational policies.

question: A multinational organization’s internal audit team is using electronic workpapers for a complex audit engagement. question: Storing records longer than needed can create an enormous challenge when an organization

options.A: Is suspected of having filed a fraudulent tax return.

question: A company is updating its document retention policy for audit workpapers. What should be considered when defining the retention period?

question: An auditor is reviewing audit document retention periods as part of the organization’s overall policy. What is the most effective way to ensure compliance with both internal and regulatory requirements?

options.C: Aligning retention schedules with legal mandates and company guidelines.
options.D: Storing only summary reports so that a longer period can be retained.

question: Which of the following concepts distinguishes the retention of computerized audit workpapers from that of the traditional hard-copy form?

options.A: Evidential support for all findings is copied and provided to local management during the closing conference and to each person receiving the final report.

options.C: Computerized data files can be used in electronic data processing audit procedures.

question: Unless part of an ongoing investigation, workpapers should typically be retained for at least how long?

options.A: The time spent on training has not been justified by the increase in productivity.

options.C: More information is needed before the success of the training program can be assessed.

question: An auditor finds during engagement planning that management’s previous audit objective focused on improving vendor relationships by reducing payment delays. However, findings showed discrepancies in invoicing processes. How should the auditor address this in the engagement conclusion?

options.B: Integrate the findings into the engagement conclusion by recommending process improvements in invoicing.
options.C: Ignore the findings because they are not directly related to the stated audit objective.

question: In evaluating the engagement results at a financial organization, an internal auditor identifies five cases in which the segregation of duties policy was not adhered to. What should be the auditor’s next step in addressing this finding?

options.A: Report the finding as a one-time error with no further investigation required.

options.C: Perform a root cause analysis to determine why the segregation of duties is not being followed.
options.D: Issue an immediate recommendation to terminate the employees involved in the segregation breach.

question: Which two terms are often used interchangeably?

options.A: “Conclusion” and “opinion.”

question:
Internal auditing is conducting an assurance audit of a regional office. An internal audit team does not suspect fraud, but it has found the following significant gaps in controls that could create opportunities for fraud:
The same individual is allowed to send invoices and receive payments.
Recordkeeping is lax.
Some documentation of expenses is missing, but the internal auditor was able to obtain documentation from vendors.
Some furniture is missing. It may have been stolen or discarded. The audit team has completed a report listing the various findings, explaining the potential for loss and fraud that these issues have created, and citing the organization’s policies and procedures. options.A: The findings do not describe conditions that could result in serious loss but are primarily procedural.

question: After performing procedures, an internal auditor’s appropriate analyses and evaluations result in

options.A: Findings.
options.B: Condition.
options.C: Engagement conclusion.
options.D: Recommendations.

question: An internal auditor’s conclusions are best described as based

options.A: Only on an entire engagement.
options.B: Only on an element of an engagement.
options.C: In part on the opinion.

question: A senior auditor is tasked with drawing conclusions from recent audit findings, including instances of noncompliance with organizational policies. What critical factor should the senior auditor consider when drawing these conclusions?

options.A: The potential effects of the findings on the organization.

options.C: The sampling methods used in the audit process.
options.D: The format of the workpaper documentation.

options.A: The age of the internal control manuals used during the audit.
options.B: The capacity of the warehouse storage facilities.
options.C: The standing operating procedures regarding inventory management.
options.D: The qualifications of the warehouse staff handling stock counts.

question: An internal audit report identified several compliance issues related to data protection laws in a financial institution. options.B: Verify the sample size and selection method to ensure this is not a sampling error before drawing conclusions.
options.C: Suggest to management that new controls need to be implemented without further investigation.
options.D: Remove these discrepancies from the audit report because they might be exceptions and not the norm.

question: An internal audit team is performing an engagement within a healthcare organization. They find that the existing electronic medical record system has lapses in data integrity checks, potentially jeopardizing patient confidentiality. As part of their engagement, what would be the most appropriate step for the audit team to take next?

options.A: Document the issue as a minor finding and recommend remedial training for staff.
options.B: Stop the audit and report the finding to regulatory authorities immediately.
options.C: Dedicate resources to perform a root cause analysis to understand the lapses in data integrity.
options.D: Ignore the finding because it seems to be an isolated incident without significant impact.

question: In a large retail organization, an internal audit identified sales records for a newly opened store that were not consistent with expected trends. The engagement supervisor needs to draw actionable conclusions based on these findings. What important aspect should the auditor consider when finalizing conclusions?

options.A: The financial targets set by the organization’s executive committee.
options.B: Peer-reviewed studies on sales trends in the retail sector.
options.C: The root causes of the discrepancies identified in sales records.
options.D: Historical sales data of other stores within the organization.

question: During an audit of procurement processes in a manufacturing firm, auditors observed unauthorized purchase orders. What should be the auditors’ primary focus to understand the significance of this finding?

options.A: Comparing the observed outcomes with the organization’s policies and procedures.
options.B: Documenting every instance of unauthorized purchase orders.
options.C: Communicating the finding to the procurement manager immediately.
options.D: Performing a detailed financial analysis to assess the impact.

question: In considering the findings of an audit about sales, the auditor discovers unauthorized discounts given by sales staff. Which approach should the auditor take to address this finding effectively?

options.A: Advise reprimanding the sales staff without further investigation.
options.B: Report this finding to senior management immediately.
options.C: Ignore the findings if the sales numbers have improved.
options.D: Investigate the reasons behind unauthorized discounts and suggest policy changes.

question: An auditor evaluating a finding notes that a control issue arose due to inadequate training of staff. What should be the auditor’s next step in the context of root cause analysis?

options.A: Recommend immediate disciplinary action for involved staff.
options.B: Evaluate the training program and suggest improvements.
options.C: Increase the sample size of audit tests related to this finding.
options.D: Document the finding without further analysis.

question: A junior auditor is performing a review for a logistics organization’s inventory control system. The auditor observed discrepancies in stock levels compared to records. What should the auditor’s initial action be to document this finding properly?

options.A: Conduct interviews with warehouse staff to understand possible causes.
options.B: Cross-reference other audits to find similar discrepancies.
options.C: Record the observed discrepancies factually in the workpapers.
options.D: Immediately recommend changes to the inventory system.

question: An auditor is evaluating the accuracy of payroll processing. What is the most effective way to identify discrepancies between existing conditions and evaluation criteria?

options.A: Conducting employee interviews to gather opinions on payroll accuracy.
options.B: Verifying payroll records against approved pay rates and recorded work hours.
options.C: Reviewing total payroll costs without analyzing individual records.
options.D: Comparing payroll expenses to the company’s projected budget.

question: An audit of expense reimbursements reveals inconsistencies in approval practices. How should the auditor determine the significance of these findings?

options.A: Measuring the financial impact and frequency and spread of noncompliance issues.
options.B: Discuss with more experienced colleagues and get their view.
options.C: Discuss with management to ascertain their level of concern.
options.D: Comparing company practices to those of external organizations.

question: During an IT security audit, an auditor discovers that some employees have broader system access than necessary for their roles. What should be considered when evaluating the severity of this issue?

options.A: The IT capabilities of those who have had access.
options.B: The longevity of service of those who have had access.
options.C: The recency of IT security training for those who had access.
options.D: Assessing the risk of unauthorized activity and potential security breaches.

question: An auditor is reviewing financial statements to determine whether recorded revenue aligns with accounting standards. What is the best method to analyze this?

options.A: Confirming that revenue amounts match internal financial projections.
options.B: Checking whether revenue trends align with management’s expectations.
options.C: Comparing revenue recognition practices to applicable financial reporting standards.
options.D: Examining a small sample of high-value transactions.

question: A compliance audit reveals that some departments are not following mandatory training requirements. What is the best approach to determine why this is happening?

options.A: Asking department heads whether employees find the training valuable.
options.B: Investigating whether training completion tracking and enforcement mechanisms are effective.
options.C: Reviewing company policies to confirm that training is listed as mandatory.
options.D: Comparing training completion rates to industry benchmarks.

question: An internal audit of inventory management identifies frequent stock shortages. How should the auditor assess the potential effects of this issue?

options.A: Analyzing data to assess impact on production delays, order fulfillment, and financial performance.
options.B: Comparing inventory levels to those of competitors.
options.C: Reviewing past audits to see if similar findings were previously reported.
options.D: Conduct interviews with a sample of operational staff to obtain their feedback.

question: A financial audit reveals that certain transactions were not approved according to company policy. What is the most effective way to identify the root cause?

options.A: Analyzing high-value transactions to determine patterns of noncompliance.
options.B: Reviewing authorization controls and approval workflows to assess enforcement.
options.C: Conducting employee interviews to evaluate awareness of approval requirements.
options.D: Consider the clarity of the job descriptions of finance staff.

question: An IT security audit finds that some employees have access to systems beyond their job requirements. What is the best approach to evaluate the impact of this issue?

options.A: Comparing system access levels to those of external organizations.
options.B: Assessing the risk of unauthorized changes, data breaches, or policy violations.
options.C: Checking if employees are aware of their additional access rights.
options.D: Reviewing recent system logs to determine actual breaches.

question: A compliance audit finds that a department consistently misses regulatory reporting deadlines. What should be analyzed to determine the significance of this finding?

options.A: Potential legal consequences and financial penalties for late submissions.
options.B: Employee feedback regarding difficulties in meeting deadlines.
options.C: Volume of regulatory reports generated annually by the organization.
options.D: Industry-wide trends in regulatory reporting timeliness.

question: A manufacturing audit uncovers inefficiencies in the production process. What is the best way to assess their significance?

options.A: Impact of delays, increased costs, and waste on overall productivity.
options.B: Level of concern communicated by employees who have reported production inefficiencies.
options.C: Trends in past production audit reports that mention workflow delays.
options.D: Industry benchmarks that outline best practices for manufacturing efficiency.

question: A financial audit identifies that revenue recognition practices do not align with accounting standards. What should be reviewed to determine the impact of this issue?

options.A: The time of year when testing identified this issue.
options.B: Justifications provided by management for their revenue recognition approach.
options.C: Effect on financial statement accuracy and compliance with regulations.
options.D: The currency of revenue recognition practices as documented in organizational policies.

question: An internal audit of corporate credit card usage finds that multiple transactions lack required supporting documentation. What should be prioritized when determining how serious this issue is?

options.A: Possibility of fraud, policy violations, and financial misstatements.
options.B: Total number of corporate credit cards issued to employees.
options.C: Prior audit reports that flagged similar documentation gaps.
options.D: Managements level of concern when initially identified.

question: An auditor has identified multiple minor control deficiencies in different departments. What is the best way to determine the overall significance of these findings?

options.A: Considering the timeframe when these deficiencies occurred.
options.B: Reporting each minor issue individually and keep a tally of the frequency.
options.C: Assessing whether the combined deficiencies indicate a larger issue.
options.D: Concluding that minor deficiencies are insignificant since they were not individually high-risk.

question: During an audit of vendor payments, an auditor identifies multiple late payments and inconsistent approvals. How should the significance of these findings be determined?

options.A: Considering the level of complaints received.
options.B: Comparing the late payments to those of industry competitors.
options.C: Documenting only the largest late payments and disregarding smaller ones.
options.D: Assessing the financial impact, compliance risks, and potential control weaknesses.

question: An internal audit of cybersecurity controls finds several instances of improper access provisioning. What factor is most important when determining the significance of this issue?

options.A: Number of access violations recorded.
options.B: Evaluations of risk and potential effect on data security.
options.C: Level of employee attendance at security training.
options.D: Currency of IT security policies.

question: An auditor has aggregated findings related to inefficiencies in the financial close process. What should be considered to determine their overall significance?

options.A: The opinions of management on whether the inefficiencies should be reported.
options.B: The number of employees involved in the financial close process.
options.C: The length of time the inefficiencies have existed without causing major issues.
options.D: The impact on reporting accuracy, timeliness, and regulatory compliance.

question: A governance audit reveals that management does not consistently act on audit recommendations. What conclusion should the auditor consider?

options.A: Strong governance because recommendations are acknowledged.
options.B: Weak governance due to inadequate follow-up and accountability.
options.C: Acceptable governance since some recommendations are progressing.
options.D: Strong governance because risks have not materialized despite control failings.

question: When engagements are performed for the internal audit function by nonstaff members, the chief audit executive is responsible for

options.A: Ensuring that the engagement communications are objective, clear, and timely.
options.B: Reviewing the engagement work programs for approval.
options.C: Providing appropriate supervision from the beginning to the conclusion of the engagement.
options.D: None of the engagement work performed by those outside the department.

question: The best control over the work on which internal auditors’ conclusions are based is

options.A: Supervisory review of all engagement work.
options.B: Preparation of time budgets for internal audit activities.
options.C: Preparation of engagement workpapers.
options.D: Staffing of the internal audit function.

question: Which of the following best describes engagement supervision?

options.A: The manager of each engagement has the ultimate responsibility for supervision.
options.B: Supervision is primarily exercised at the final review stage of an engagement to ensure the accuracy of the engagement communications.
options.C: Supervision is most important in the planning phase of the engagement to ensure appropriate coverage.
options.D: Supervision is a continuing process beginning with planning and ending with the conclusion of the engagement.

question: An engagement supervisor is leading a three-person auditing team assigned to an assurance engagement at airport rental locations for a car rental company. All team members are experienced. In planning her own work schedule, the supervisor believes that it will be necessary to allow time to supervise the team during the execution phase, the planning process, and the drafting of the internal audit report. Is the supervisor taking the correct approach? Why?

options.A: No. Once planning is completed, the most critical supervisory task is review of workpapers.
options.B: No. When a team is experienced, supervision throughout the engagement is an unnecessary expense for the function.
options.C: Yes. All engagements should be closely supervised in the same manner.
options.D: Yes. Supervisory decisions must be made during all phases of the internal audit, regardless of the experience level of the team members.

question: A new staff auditor was told to perform an audit in an area with which the auditor was not familiar. Due to time constraints, the audit was not supervised. The auditor was given the assignment because it represented a good learning experience, but the area was clearly beyond the auditor’s competence. Nevertheless, the auditor prepared comprehensive workpapers and reported the results to the CAE. In this situation,

options.A: The internal audit function violated the Standards by not providing adequate supervision.
options.B: The internal audit function violated the Standards by hiring an auditor without proficiency in the area.
options.C: The CAE has not violated the Standards because they do not address supervision.
options.D: The Standards were followed by the internal audit function.

question:
A new staff internal auditor’s first assignment is to review the cash management operations of the organization. The staff internal auditor has no background in cash management. Under which of the following conditions would this arrangement be appropriate?
The engagement supervisor is skilled in the area and closely supervises the staff internal auditor.
The staff internal auditor performs the work and prepares an engagement communication that is reviewed in detail by the chief audit executive.

options.A:

Yes

options.B:

question: Which one of the following is performed by the CAE and not the engagement supervisor?

options.A: Reviewing and analyzing an engagement work program to determine whether the proposed engagement procedures will result in information relevant to the engagement’s objectives.
options.B: Assuring that an engagement communication is supported and accurate relative to the information documented in the engagement workpapers.
options.C: Using risk assessment and other judgmental processes to develop an engagement work schedule for the internal audit function and present the schedule to the board.
options.D: Determining that staff auditors have completed the engagement procedures and that engagement objectives have been met.

question: The engagement supervisor is least likely to have a primary role in

options.A: Allocating budgeted engagement hours among assigned staff.
options.B: Updating the permanent files.
options.C: Reviewing the workpapers.
options.D: Preparing the critique sheet for the engagement.

question: Which of the following statements regarding supervision of the work of internal auditors is true?

options.A: The engagement supervisor has ultimate responsibility for supervising the internal auditors.
options.B: Supervisory tasks may not be delegated.
options.C: Supervision includes providing feedback to the internal auditors but does not extend to the development of competencies.
options.D: The extent of supervision needs to be documented.

question: Which of the following best describes what determines the extent of supervision required for a particular internal audit engagement?

options.A: Whether the engagement involves possible fraud on the part of management.
options.B: Whether the engagement involves possible violations of laws or governmental regulations.
options.C: The proficiency of the internal auditors and the complexity of the engagement.
options.D: The internal audit function’s prior experience in dealing with the particular department.

question: During a meeting of an internal audit project team, two members of the team disagree, and one accuses the other of trying to advance personal interests over the interests of the audit. The engagement supervisor should

options.A: Discipline both auditors after the meeting for their lack of professional conduct.
options.B: Continue the meeting but speak to the accusing auditor later regarding the inappropriate conduct.
options.C: Meet with both auditors after the meeting to resolve the conflict and the inappropriate behavior.
options.D: Stop the meeting and refer the matter to the entire team for discussion.

question: The CAE is trying to explain the range of responsibilities a senior internal auditor will be assuming as supervisor of an upcoming engagement that will employ a team of internal auditors. All of the following are examples that the CAE is likely to mention except

options.A: Training less experienced team members in appropriate audit procedures.
options.B: Establishing a process to ensure timely communication of necessary information among team members.
options.C: Assuming ultimate responsibility for adequate supervision during the engagement.
options.D: Assigning team members to specific roles and procedures.

question:
A senior internal auditor is explaining the responsibilities of engagement supervision to a newly-hired junior auditor. The senior auditor mentions the following responsibilities:
Specific activities are prescribed in the Standards.
The extent varies depending on the proficiency of the internal auditors.
The extent varies depending on the complexity of the engagement.
The engagement supervisor has primary responsibility for supervision.
Which of the responsibilities listed are correct?

options.A: Specific activities are prescribed in the Standards only.
options.B: Specific activities are prescribed in the Standards, and the extent varies depending on the complexity of the engagement only.
options.C: Specific activities are prescribed in the Standards, and the engagement supervisor has primary responsibility for supervision only.
options.D: Specific activities are prescribed in the Standards, and the extent varies depending on the proficiency of the internal auditors and the complexity of the engagement only.

question: A supervisor at a retail organization’s internal audit department needs to assign tasks to each internal auditor in the department for an upcoming engagement. What should the supervisor primarily focus on to ensure effective task allocation?

options.A: Assigning tasks to the most efficient auditors only to ensure timely completion.
options.B: Matching tasks with each auditor’s proficiency and experience.
options.C: Assigning higher-profile tasks to more experienced auditors only.
options.D: Alternating task assignments to ensure role variety.

question: While supervising an internal audit of a utilities company, the supervisor realizes that the planned audit objectives are not aligned with the board’s updated strategic goals. What should be the immediate action taken by the supervisor?

options.A: Reallocate resources to more critical objectives.
options.B: Adjust the objectives immediately to align with strategic goals.
options.C: Notify the board after the audit completion.
options.D: Postpone the audit until the supervisor believes there is organization-wide buy-in for the updated strategic goals.

question: An internal audit team is preparing for an engagement at a financial institution. During the engagement planning phase, the chief audit executive (CAE) delegates supervisory tasks to a team member based on the complexity of the engagement and the member’s proficiency. Which supervisory task is most crucial to delegate to ensure the effectiveness of the engagement?

options.A: Approving the engagement work program.
options.B: Allocating resources to audit tasks.
options.C: Reviewing the final audit report.
options.D: Coordinating communication with stakeholders.

question: If an audit supervisor identifies a significant misalignment between the audit objective and the organizational goal during an engagement, what should the supervisor do to correct this?

options.A: Continue the audit as planned, assuming minor goals can be realigned later.
options.B: Consult with the chief audit executive to redefine the audit objectives and ensure alignment.
options.C: Document the misalignment in the final report for further review by the audit committee.
options.D: Reassign audit resources to other areas and postpone the current audit.

question: In an auditing department of a manufacturing company, the supervising auditor realizes that the audit team has seldom utilized the internal control framework endorsed by the company. Which of the following actions would be most beneficial in integrating this framework effectively into the audit engagements?

options.A: Hire an experienced internal auditor who is an expert in the framework.
options.B: Provide comprehensive training on the internal control framework to the audit team.
options.C: Mandate the inclusion of the framework in future audit reports.
options.D: Utilize external consultants who have experience using the framework.

question: While leading an audit engagement in a non-profit organization, the engagement supervisor discovers that the initial risk assessment was significantly underestimated. What step should the supervisor take to address this issue appropriately?

options.A: Proceed with the existing plan.
options.B: Adjust the engagement plan immediately to address the identified risks.
options.C: Report the underestimated assessment to senior management but make no changes.
options.D: Adjust the timeline of the audit engagement due to the risk assessment error.

question: A financial service company is conducting an internal audit to evaluate its compliance with regulatory requirements. The engagement supervisor identifies that one of the auditors lacks expertise in the specific compliance regulations being audited. How should the engagement supervisor address this issue?

options.A: Allow the auditor to complete the task and gain experience.
options.B: Pair the auditor with a more knowledgeable team member for guidance.
options.C: Reassign the auditor to a supporting administrative role for this audit.
options.D: Postpone the audit and provide training to the auditor on the relevant regulations.

question: An internal auditor is preparing an engagement work program for an audit of a manufacturing company’s inventory management process. The auditor has limited experience in this complexity of engagement. What should the engagement supervisor prioritize to ensure the objectives are achieved, and quality standards are maintained?

options.A: Assign the auditor additional tasks to broaden their experience.
options.B: Review and approve the work program before execution, ensuring it aligns with risk assessments.
options.C: Schedule frequent meetings to discuss progress.
options.D: Replace the auditor with a more experienced team member immediately.

question: During an internal audit engagement at a large manufacturing company, the lead auditor discovers discrepancies in inventory counts. What is the lead auditor’s responsibility in addressing this situation?

options.A: Inform the chief financial officer immediately and suggest adjustments to the financial statements.
options.B: Conduct further audit testing to determine the cause and extent of discrepancies and document any findings in the engagement workpapers.
options.C: Report the findings to the external auditors and let them handle the discrepancies.
options.D: Recommend engaging an external inventory specialist to redo the counts.

question: A department within an organization is resistant to the audit process, complicating the engagement. As the engagement supervisor, how would you handle this resistance?

options.A: Escalate the issue to senior management immediately.
options.B: Adjust the audit scope to avoid resistance-related areas.
options.C: Communicate the audit’s value and seek to understand the department’s concerns.
options.D: Proceed with the audit as planned and document the department’s resistance.

question: An engagement is running behind schedule due to uneven workload distribution among auditors. What should the supervisor do to address this issue?

options.A: Extending the audit timeline to accommodate the delays.
options.B: Rebalancing assignments to ensure work is evenly distributed among the team.
options.C: Requiring auditors to work longer hours to complete their tasks.
options.D: Reducing the scope of the audit to meet deadlines.

question: A newly assigned auditor is struggling with a complex task. What is the most appropriate action for the supervisor?

options.A: Reassigning the auditor to a different engagement without addressing the challenge.
options.B: Providing guidance and adjusting the task if necessary to align with the auditor’s capabilities.
options.C: Allowing the auditor to work independently without intervention.
options.D: Reallocating the auditors other tasks so that they have more time.

question: An audit supervisor is coordinating fieldwork assignments for a remote audit. What is a key consideration when assigning tasks?

options.A: Assigning tasks based on the auditors’ time zones without considering expertise.
options.B: Ensuring that all auditors have access to necessary systems and data for remote work.
options.C: Requiring all auditors to work on-site to avoid coordination issues.
options.D: Rotating auditors frequently to allow exposure to multiple areas.

question: A supervisor is responsible for coordinating work assignments across multiple audit locations. What is an essential factor to consider?

options.A: Variety–rotating auditors to different locations maintains their independence.
options.B: Setting goals and delegating authority to each location lead.
options.C: The auditors’ preferences of assignment–a happy auditor is a productive one.
options.D: Establishing clear communication channels to manage workflow effectively.

question: A supervisor notices that an auditor is struggling with a complex audit procedure. What is the most effective approach?

options.A: Providing coaching, guidance, and additional resources to support the auditor.
options.B: Removing the auditor from the task and assigning it to a more experienced colleague.
